newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac plays Europe card in French election.
newsitem.headline: Chirac plays Europe card in French election.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac has played the Europe card in the final days of France's parliamentary election campaign, hoping to catch out the left-wing opposition and take the pressure off unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
But it remains to be seen whether it will prove a joker or a dud with an electorate tempted by Euroscepticm.
Chirac used a Paris visit by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday to issue a barely concealed warning to voters that electing a left-wing government would weaken France's voice in Europe.

"Let us never forget that (France) will only be able to defend its interests if it is capable of speaking with a single voice, a strong voice," the conservative president said in a message broadcast on prime-time television news.

He vowed to guarantee France's European commitments, a clear reference to the planned single currency, and implied that a victory for the Socialists and Communists would jeopardise European integration.

While refusing to comment on French politics, Kohl gave Chirac a hand by ruling out any renegotiation of the so-called stability pact agreed by EU leaders last December to limit the budget deficits of countries that join the single currency.
Socialist Lionel Jospin has said he would seek to renegotiate the terms for European economic and monetary union if the left wins the election.
Conservative commentators said Chirac was right to dramatise the dangers of "cohabitation", as the French call power-sharing between a president and a government of opposite parties.
Left-wing editorialists denounced "European blackmail" -- a term used in both the Communist daily L'Humanite and the daily Liberation.

Political analyst Alain Duhamel said Chirac's decision to play the Europe card was a pitch to middle-class voters, who are strongly pro-European but are tempted to vote Socialist in protest against austerity policies.

But other commentators said many voters seemed more attracted by Jospin's "yes, but" to European monetary union, rejecting further austerity to meet the conditions for a single currency, than by Chirac's "yes at any price".

Jospin sought to defuse the issue immediately by saying it was self-evident that France would continue to speak with a single voice if the left won, just as it had during two previous periods of "cohabitation" under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
But the exchange highlighted the division between the Socialists' conditional support for the euro and the Communists' opposition to a single currency.

When Chirac dissolved parliament on April 21 and called a snap poll, he cited the need to strengthen France's position in forthcoming decisions on European Union reform, the single currency and the eastward enlargement of the EU and NATO.
But until Tuesday, the issue had largely slipped off the campaign agenda, which was dominated by unemployment, economic policy and the fate of Juppe himself.
Opinion polls show two-thirds of voters want Chirac to get rid of Juppe, whom they blame for the austerity policies required to qualify for the single currency in 1999.

Playing the Europe card allows the president to dominate the final days of the campaign and take the focus off the premier. He will have two more opportunities to shine on the European stage in the next week.

Chirac will attend an informal EU summit on Friday in the Dutch resort of Noordwijk. Diplomats said it was switched at French insistence from the symbolic venue of Maastricht, which gave its name to the 1993 treaty on European union, to avoid upsetting Eurosceptical voters.
The timing gives Chirac the last word before the first round of voting when he holds a news conference after official election campaigning ends in France.

Then, next Tuesday, he will play host to U.S. President Bill Clinton, Russian President Boris Yeltsin and NATO leaders for the signing of a landmark partnership agreement between the Atlantic Alliance and Russia, trumpeted by France as finally ending the division of Europe set by the 1945 Yalta summit.

Historians recalled that it was Mitterrand who first used the phrase "France speaks with a single voice" in 1986 to assert his primacy over Chirac, who was then prime minister under the first "cohabitation".
